claim: Fever drives elimination of invading microorganisms through microbicidal disease resistance while hypothermia promotes tolerance to foster energy conservation and management of collateral inflammation-associated tissue damage.
source: Although both reflect an animal's capacity to take advantage of thermoregulation to maintain fitness upon infection, fever drives elimination of invading microorganisms through microbicidal disease resistance while hypothermia promotes tolerance to foster energy conservation and management of collateral inflammation-associated tissue damage (Steiner and Romanovsky, 2019; Wang and Medzhitov, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steiner and Romanovsky, 2019; Wang and Medzhitov, 2019

claim: Fever promoted disease resistance via enhanced kinetics of leukocyte recruitment rather than by augmenting the magnitude or duration of immune activation.
source: Early on, fever promoted disease resistance via enhanced kinetics of leukocyte recruitment rather than by augmenting the magnitude or duration of immune activation.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Engagement of cytoprotective gene programmes in the CNS occurred within hours of the initial immune challenge.
source: Engagement of cytoprotective gene programmes in the CNS occurred within hours of the initial immune challenge.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Selective rather than global upregulation of immunity decreased the potential for collateral damage often attributed to fever.
source: Selective rather than global upregulation of immunity further decreased the potential for collateral damage often attributed to fever.
evidence: Inference based on data shown in Figures 4D, 4E, and 5

claim: Microbicidal efficacy was superior under fever, with Aeromonas clearance achieved markedly faster than under thermally restricted basal conditions (7 vs. 14 days).
source: Notably, microbicidal efficacy was still superior under fever, with Aeromonas clearance achieved markedly faster than under thermally restricted basal conditions (7 vs. 14 days).
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Fever actively engages mechanisms that enhance protection, while also limiting pathology, controlling inflammation, and promoting tissue repair.
source: Thus, fever actively engages mechanisms that enhance protection, while also limiting pathology, controlling inflammation, and promoting tissue repair.
evidence: Inference based on data shown throughout the manuscript

claim: Fever is an integrative host response to infection that regulates both induction and resolution phases of acute inflammation.
source: To conclude, our results reveal novel features of fever, and demonstrate that it is an integrative host response to infection that regulates both induction and resolution phases of acute inflammation.
evidence: Inference based on data shown throughout the manuscript

claim: This integrative strategy emerged prior to endothermy during evolution.
source: Together, our results define fever as an integrative host response that regulates induction and resolution of acute inflammation, and demonstrate that this integrative strategy emerged prior to endothermy during evolution.
evidence: Inference based on demonstration of integrative fever response in ectothermic fish

claim: Goldfish offer an opportunity to examine absolute changes to thermopreference to an immune challenge, while minimizing the potential for thermal stress.
source: As eurythermal ectotherms, goldfish offered an opportunity to examine absolute changes to thermopreference to an immune challenge, while minimizing the potential for thermal stress.
evidence: Inference based on goldfish biology

claim: The natural range of tolerated environmental temperatures for goldfish is 1.3–34.5°C.
source: This is because the natural range of tolerated environmental temperatures for these fish (1.3–34.5°C) was broader than those temperatures expected in a febrile response.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of goldfish thermal tolerance

claim: A custom swim chamber, coupled to high-fidelity quantitative positional tracking, showed remarkable consistency in fish behaviours and defined the febrile window.
source: A custom swim chamber, coupled to high-fidelity quantitative positional tracking, showed remarkable consistency in fish behaviours and defined the febrile window.
evidence: Based on behavioral data shown in Figure 2

claim: Animals exerting fever engaged pyrogenic cytokine gene programmes in the central nervous system.
source: Animals exerting fever engaged pyrogenic cytokine gene programmes in the central nervous system, increased efficiency of leukocyte recruitment into the immune challenge site, and markedly improved pathogen clearance in vivo, even when an infecting bacterium grew better at higher temperatures.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Animals exerting fever increased efficiency of leukocyte recruitment into the immune challenge site.
source: Animals exerting fever engaged pyrogenic cytokine gene programmes in the central nervous system, increased efficiency of leukocyte recruitment into the immune challenge site, and markedly improved pathogen clearance in vivo, even when an infecting bacterium grew better at higher temperatures.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Animals exerting fever markedly improved pathogen clearance in vivo, even when an infecting bacterium grew better at higher temperatures.
source: Animals exerting fever engaged pyrogenic cytokine gene programmes in the central nervous system, increased efficiency of leukocyte recruitment into the immune challenge site, and markedly improved pathogen clearance in vivo, even when an infecting bacterium grew better at higher temperatures.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figures 4A and 4B

claim: Selectivity in the protective immune mechanisms activated through fever was identified, contrary to earlier speculations for global upregulation of immunity.
source: Contrary to earlier speculations for global upregulation of immunity, we identified selectivity in the protective immune mechanisms activated through fever.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figures 4D and 4E

claim: Fever inhibited inflammation and markedly improved wound repair.
source: Fever then inhibited inflammation and markedly improved wound repair.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7

claim: Artificial mechanical hyperthermia recapitulated some but not all benefits achieved through natural host-driven dynamic thermoregulation.
source: Artificial mechanical hyperthermia, often used as a model of fever, recapitulated some but not all benefits achieved through natural host-driven dynamic thermoregulation.
evidence: Based on comparison of TD and TS26 data throughout the manuscript

claim: Fever differentially regulated ROS and NO leukocyte antimicrobial mechanisms in Aeromonas-challenged fish.
source: Thus, fever differentially regulated ROS and NO leukocyte antimicrobial mechanisms in Aeromonas-challenged fish.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figures 4D and 4E

claim: Fever promoted an earlier pro-inflammatory period, which was paired with more efficient resolution of inflammation based on inhibition of leukocyte recruitment, control of pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, induction of pro-resolution genes, and management of collateral tissue damage.
source: Thus, fever promoted an earlier pro-inflammatory period, which was further paired with more efficient resolution of inflammation based on inhibition of leukocyte recruitment, control of pro-inflammatory cytokine expression, induction of pro-resolution genes, and management of collateral tissue damage.
evidence: Based on data shown in Figures 4C, 5A, and 5B
